## Discussion {#sec-discussion}

I take up the welfare consequences of preemption, the model's testable predictions, its policy implications, and its limitations.

### Welfare and Overinvestment

I do not solve a planner's problem, so the model characterizes no social optimum; the benchmark it computes is the monopolist's policy. Against that benchmark competition brings investment forward. At baseline a monopolist that chooses its scale when the switch arrives waits for it, whereas in the entry game one firm invests before the switch, at $X_L$, and the other waits for the switch and enters after it (Proposition 3, @fig-competition-effect). Whether industry capacity exceeds what two firms would install cooperatively, and so whether competition dissipates rents on net, requires a benchmark I do not compute.

### Testable Predictions

The model generates three cross-sectional predictions and one conjecture, testable in principle on the small cross-section of frontier AI labs. I write $\phi^{\mathrm{o}}$ for a lab's measured share of compute devoted to training, an empirical object distinct from the model's allocation $\phi$ and from the training fractions $\hat{\phi}$ assigned to the archetypes in @sec-calibration. Each item names the model object it rests on and whether the property used is analytical or numerical.

1. Training-heavy labs should carry less credit risk, through the default probability and not through recovery. Conditional on leverage, capacity, and demand, a lab whose higher $\phi^{\mathrm{o}}$ reflects an expectation of an earlier switch should sit further from its default boundary. The object is the closed-form boundary of Proposition 2 (single-boundary reduction): at a fixed allocation it falls in $\lambda$ if and only if $\phi > \tilde{\phi}$, analytically, and along the model's allocation $\phi^*(\lambda)$ the allocation's own effect vanishes because $\phi^*$ minimizes the boundary, so the boundary falls with optimism wherever $\phi^* > \tilde{\phi}$, which holds for $\lambda \gtrsim 0.034$ at baseline. At a given belief, the spread falls as the training fraction rises over $\phi \in [0.30, 0.75]$ at the single firm's and the leader's scale and entry demand, under both debt conventions (@fig-credit-risk, numerical). The model does not predict that training-heavy labs recover less in default: at its policies recovery is at most $5\%$ of the claim and rises with $\phi$ (@sec-valuation, numerical), so the loss given default is close to total whatever the allocation.
2. Firms with higher $\phi^{\mathrm{o}}$ should have higher equity betas, under the auxiliary assumption, imported from @aguerrevere2009real, that the H-regime component of value carries the higher systematic-risk loading; the model itself discounts every claim at a single rate $r$ and has no pricing kernel, so this is a conjecture about value composition rather than a model implication. Because composition here shifts with the training-inference split at a given capacity, $\phi^{\mathrm{o}}$ should carry explanatory power beyond capacity and concentration measures.
3. The value of an installed lab should respond asymmetrically to timeline news. The object is the value of a firm that has invested and holds its capacity and allocation fixed when beliefs change, not the value of the unexercised option in @fig-lambda-option-value. Its going-concern value $A_{\text{eff}}(\lambda) X - \delta K/r$ is increasing and strictly concave in $\lambda$ at every arrival rate when $\phi > \underline{\phi} \approx 0.18$, so news that lengthens expected timelines lowers it by more than news of the same size that shortens them raises it (Corollary 1, Internet Appendix A, analytical); below $\underline{\phi}$ it falls in $\lambda$ and the asymmetry reverses. With the option to stop, for unlevered value and for levered equity, and for the duopoly leader, whose value also carries the follower's dilution, the same shape holds numerically at the model's policies and on the grid of Internet Appendix A, away from the boundary; it fails close to the boundary and, for the leader, at low training fractions. At a common belief the sensitivity and the asymmetry rise with the training fraction (Corollary 1(iii)). Across labs whose training fractions differ because their beliefs differ they do not: at the model's allocation the semi-elasticity of revenue value in $\lambda$ is $2.25$ at $\lambda = 0.10$ and $0.30$ at $\lambda = 0.50$, so the most optimistic labs are the least exposed to timeline news.
4. Training shares should rise with beliefs about AI timelines, and capacity should not be a monotone proxy for those beliefs. The single firm's $\phi^*$ increases in $\lambda$ in closed form (Proposition 1(i)). In the entry game the leader's $\phi_L$ also rises with $\lambda$ at every arrival rate on the grid and lies below $\phi^*$ by $14\%$ at $\lambda = 0.03$, $3.1\%$ at baseline and $0.2\%$ at $\lambda = 0.50$ (Proposition 3(ii), numerical), while the date and the scale of the first investment are hump-shaped in $\lambda$, with a maximum near $0.15$ (Proposition 3(iv), numerical). Competitive position therefore lowers the training share of a lab that invests before the switch by little except at long timelines, and a lab that enters after the switch trains with all its capacity (Proposition 3(i)). Controlling for technology, $\phi^{\mathrm{o}}$ should order labs by beliefs where capital expenditure need not.

These predictions are directional, and the small cross-section currently limits formal testing: default-probability and spread regressions on training-compute proxies could test prediction 1, event studies around capability releases and forecast revisions could test prediction 3, and regressions of training shares and capital expenditure on belief proxies could test prediction 4.

### Policy Implications

The model bears on financial stability, competition policy, and disclosure, though in each case it supports a narrower claim than the policy question requires. On financial stability, irreversible investment, leverage, and regime-dependent demand compress the firm's margin of safety at entry (@sec-model, @sec-valuation), and the faith-based survival channel (Proposition 2) makes solvency depend on a belief parameter, so at the calibrated optimum, where $\phi^* > \tilde{\phi}$, a downward revision in $\lambda$ would raise the default boundary and cut equity value simultaneously; with no asset market and no feedback from liquidation onto prices, the model cannot take the further step to fire sales or contagion. On competition policy, competition brings the first investment forward (at baseline the monopolist waits for the switch, while the leader of the entry game invests before it, @sec-duopoly), and the leader's date and scale of entry are hump-shaped in $\lambda$, so capacity announcements are weak evidence about timeline beliefs. On disclosure, $\phi$ jointly determines the default boundary and the composition of firm value (Propositions 1 and 2), so an investor working inside this model would need the training share $\phi^{\mathrm{o}}$, not compute spending alone, to locate a lab relative to its default boundary.

### Limitations

The static training fraction is the model's sharpest simplification, and a two-period extension in Internet Appendix E (@tbl-dynamic-phi) signs and bounds the resulting bias. The bias is not a drift in the allocation over time, since the switch time is exponential and the firm learns nothing from its non-arrival; it is the value of the option to *re-purpose* compute at the switch, which biases the pre-switch allocation downward. The static model is the polar case in which the whole H-regime prize must be bought in advance, so its $\phi^* \approx 0.70$ is an *upper bound*. That exercise solves allocation and value only, not default or belief mismatch, so what it says about the headline mechanisms is a conjecture rather than a result. The Proposition 2 solvency floor runs through the *level* of pre-switch training, which the lower $\phi_1$ would attenuate. For the Numerical Finding 1 asymmetry the direction is open: re-purposing lets an over-trainer recover, which lowers the optimistic loss, and lets an under-trainer catch up, which lowers the pessimistic one. An extension in which capability, and not compute, has to be in place at the switch (Internet Appendix E, @tbl-capability) keeps the pre-switch training fraction positive under free redeployment as long as capability built late is worth less than $57\%$ of capability in place; on its grid the pessimistic error remains the costlier one for equal errors in $\lambda$ and not for equal proportional errors.

The training technology is stylized in four further respects. Training earns no revenue in regime $L$ and post-switch revenue requires no inference capacity, a knife-edge that sharpens the allocation trade-off; in practice inference demand likely remains large after the switch and training raises pre-AGI revenue, which would attenuate it. Training is a flow allocation of installed capacity rather than an accumulated stock of capability, so there is no learning curve. Capacity is installed once, as a single irreversible lump. Inference-time scaling also blurs the training-inference boundary the model treats as sharp.

The arrival rate $\lambda$ is exogenous. A natural extension would make it a function of aggregate training compute. I do not solve it, and what follows is a conjecture rather than a result: a decentralized equilibrium would plausibly leave that spillover partly uninternalized, so equilibrium training could fall short of what a coordinating industry would choose, and the two forces would then run in opposite directions, preemption toward overinvestment in capacity and the spillover toward underinvestment in training.

Leverage is a stress-test parameter rather than an equilibrium financing choice. @leland1994corporate assumes publicly traded equity and continuously tradeable debt, whereas frontier AI labs reportedly finance themselves with SAFE notes, convertible debt, and multi-class equity. The mechanism is best read as a tractable approximation to the distress risk these firms face: $X_D$ is the demand level at which the firm can no longer sustain operations, whether the binding constraint is a missed coupon, a failed funding round, or a covenant violation. Par issuance at $r_c < r$ also implies a financing subsidy the model does not endogenize.

Finally, the Tullock contest function is a reduced form that abstracts from product differentiation, network effects, and switching costs, and it omits the market-growing effect of AI adoption, which biases the model toward stronger competition effects; the Cournot alternative is discussed in @sec-duopoly and Internet Appendix E. All valuation uses the reduced-form risk-adjusted framework of @sec-model and Internet Appendix B, a certainty-equivalent convention rather than a pricing measure, so, with a positive risk premium on demand and the default boundary held fixed, physical default probabilities would be lower.
